Introduction
❑ Binomial name: Spodoptera FRUGIPERDA
• Phylum – Arthropoda, Class – Insecta, Order –
Lepidoptera, Family – Noctuidae, Genus – Spodoptera
• Species – S. frugiperda
❑ Fall armyworm (FAW), Spodoptera frugiperda - native to 
tropical and subtropical regions of the Western 
Hemisphere;
❑ The multiple generations, the ability to migrate, and wide 
host range makes FAW one of the most severe economic 
pests;
❑ First reported in West and Central Africa 2016, now spread 
to most states in Nigeria;
❑ FAW threatens food security and livelihoods.

Host Damage
• Fall armyworm generally feeds on foliage, but during 
heavy infestations, larvae will also feed on maize ears; 
• Damage signs:
➢ Foliar damage to maize - ragged feeding, and moist 
sawdust-like frass near the whorl and upper leaves of 
the plant;
➢ Ear damage - chewed kernels and visible frass. FAW 
tends to burrow through the husk instead of feeding 
down through the silks.

▪ Basic Considerations
➢ Understanding how FAW breed, 
travel and feed - critical to 
management; 
▪ Several characteristics that make 
FAW particularly hard to control 
includes the fact that: 
✓ the moths are strong flyers;
✓ moths breed at an astonishingly 
high rate (laying >1000 eggs during 
their lifetime);

✓ larvae can feed on a particularly 
wide range of host plant (100 spp. 
in 27 families);
✓ FAW has tendency to build up 
resistance to pesticides. 
How to Control Fall Army Worm

label: page 13
page 14
text:
▪ Important considerations
✓Insecticide application - eggs are present on 5% 
of seedlings or when 25% of plants show signs of 
feeding damage; 
✓Since the greatest damage usually occurs 
before the reproductive phase of maize, early 
pest detection that allows insecticide treatment 
of young larval stages is crucial;
✓To be effective, insecticide application should 
commence before larvae burrow into the whorls 
or ears and insecticide spray should penetrate the 
crop canopy.
▪ Recommended Insecticides
➢ Pyrethroids, carbamates and organophosphates
➢ Biorational insecticides ( abamectin, spinosad, 
spinoteram, Insect Growth Regulators, etc.);
➢ Locally available botanical insecticides
▪ Recommended Insecticide Application Rate
➢ Lambda super/cyhalothrin - 100ml/15litre of 
water (tank of knapsack sprayer).
➢ Cymethoate 50ml -100mls/15 litres of water, 
Consider 30ml- 50mls/15 litres of water.
➢ Karate 15mls -20mls /15litre of water.
➢ Sumitox or chlorpyrifos - 80mls -100ml/15litre of 
water.
➢ Sharp-shooter (Profenofos 40%+ Cypermethrin) 
– 15 mls/15 liters of water
Chemical Control

label: page 15
text:
▪ Sharp -Shooter insecticide is a systemic broad 
spectrum pyrethroid commonly used in Nigeria; 
▪ The active ingredients are Profenofos and 
Cypermethrin;
▪ Cypermethrin ensures that the target pests are 
killed almost instantly upon assimilation of the 
insecticide while Profenofos works systemically;
▪ When using Sharp- Shooter insecticide:
▪ Use a clean knapsack sprayer.
▪ Half fill the sprayer with clean water.
▪ Add 1 litre of the insecticide to 200 litres of 
water. 
▪ Pour 15 litres of the solution into a 15-litre 
knapsack sprayer.
▪ Shake the knapsack sprayer for the insecticide 
to mix well with the water.
▪ Fill up the knapsack with clean water and shake 
vigorously to mix well.
▪ Carry the knapsack sprayer on your back and 
spray all the surfaces of the plants and the soil if 
need be. 
▪ Ensure to spray the plants well once a week.
▪ For highly infested farms, it can be applied to 
crops 2 – 3 times in a week.
▪ Spray in the evenings through nights when FAW 
are more exposed to the spray
▪ The first application on the plants should be 35-
45 days after planting.

Field Monitoring 
➢ Do they have a nice dark green color (indicating good 
nutrition)?, 
➢ Do they appear moisture-stressed?, 
➢ Are there signs of damage (from FAW, other insects, or 
diseases)?, 
➢ If there is FAW damage, is it current (look into the whorl 
and see if there are holes in leaves in the whorl and fresh 
frass)? 
➢ Are there FAW egg masses present? Young larvae?
➢ Are there farmers’ friends present (ants, wasps, larvae 
killed by pathogens)?
▪ A pheromone trap attracts male insects; 
▪ The Universal Bucket Trap is normally used; 
▪ The traps and the lure can usually be obtained locally, or 
from your local extension office.

label: page 19
text:
Simple Actions Required
▪ Simple actions 
✓ Mechanically killing FAW eggs and young larvae (Eggs 
masses and young larvae picked off and crushed);
▪ Try local solutions:
✓ Recycling pathogens (natural killed by virus, fungi or 
bacteria in the field);
✓ Attract predators & parasitoids ( ants, wasps);
✓ Local substances (soil, ash, sand, lime, salt, soaps, oils, 
and local plants extracts etc.) applied directly to whorl 
of infested plants.
